definitions.definition: An educated guess that you test with experiments.
definitions.example: Like saying 'plants grow faster with music' and then testing it.

definitions.definition: The tendency to look for evidence that supports what you already believe and ignore evidence that doesn't.
definitions.example: If you think a coin is lucky, you remember the times it lands heads and forget the tails.

definitions.definition: When an idea contradicts itself or proves itself wrong.
definitions.example: Saying 'I never tell the truth' is self-refuting because if it's true, it's false.

definitions.definition: An endless chain of causes or reasons that never reaches a starting point.
definitions.example: If you say 'I know it because my teacher said so, and she knows it because her teacher said so...' that goes on forever.

definitions.definition: When an idea disagrees with what we observe in the real world through experiments or measurements.
definitions.example: Claiming water freezes at 100°C is an empirical contradiction because we see it freeze at 0°C.

definitions.definition: When parts of an argument don't fit together or make sense as a whole.
definitions.example: Saying 'I am both taller and shorter than you' is logically incoherent.

definitions.definition: When an idea cannot explain the thing it's supposed to explain.
definitions.example: A theory of gravity that can't explain why apples fall has explanatory failure.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that gravity is caused by mass bending space and time, like a heavy ball on a trampoline.
definitions.example: It explains why planets orbit the sun and why GPS needs adjustments.

definitions.definition: Ripples in space-time caused by massive objects moving, like waves from a rock thrown in a pond.
definitions.example: When two black holes crash, they send gravitational waves across the universe.

definitions.definition: Points in space-time where gravity is so strong that the normal laws of physics break down, like the center of a black hole.
definitions.example: A black hole's center is a singularity where matter is crushed to an infinitely small point.

definitions.definition: The idea that gravity and acceleration feel exactly the same; you can't tell them apart in a small room.
definitions.example: In an elevator accelerating upward, you feel heavier, just like in stronger gravity.

definitions.definition: A basic truth that is accepted without proof, used as a starting point for other reasoning.
definitions.example: In math, 'the shortest distance between two points is a straight line' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: Something that is true but has no explanation for why it's true; it just is.
definitions.example: Why does the universe exist? Some say it's a brute fact with no deeper reason.

definitions.definition: When an argument uses its conclusion as one of its premises, going in a circle.
definitions.example: Saying 'the Bible is true because it says it's true' is circular.

definitions.definition: A type of math that studies curved surfaces and spaces, like the surface of a sphere or a saddle.
definitions.example: It's used to describe the curved shape of space-time in Einstein's theory.

definitions.definition: In math, a space that looks flat and smooth when you zoom in, like the surface of Earth looks flat from your backyard.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee cup are both smooth manifolds because they have no sharp edges.

definitions.definition: The law that the total amount of energy and momentum in the universe stays the same; they can't be created or destroyed.
definitions.example: When you throw a ball, your energy goes into the ball's motion; the total energy stays constant.

definitions.definition: The slow, extra rotation of Mercury's orbit around the sun that Einstein's theory perfectly predicted.
definitions.example: Mercury's orbit shifts a tiny bit each year, and only General Relativity explains the exact amount.

definitions.definition: The shortest or straightest path between two points on a curved surface, like a great circle route on Earth.
definitions.example: Airplanes fly along geodesics to save fuel, curving with the Earth's shape.

definitions.definition: When two different things have the same structure or pattern, so you can swap labels and they work the same way.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system and the actual subway lines are isomorphic in terms of connections.

definitions.definition: A way for computers to find patterns in complex data by assuming it lies on a curved surface.
definitions.example: It's like finding that a pile of photos of faces actually lies on a smooth 'face space'.

definitions.definition: A branch of math that uses curved spaces to measure how much information data gives about a model.
definitions.example: It helps statisticians understand how certain they can be about their guesses from data.

definitions.definition: When two systems have the same underlying structure, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A family tree and a company's org chart can be structurally isomorphic if both have a boss at the top.
